questions.prompt: Which statement about Redis Bitmaps is correct?

options.text: They are a distinct data type separate from strings
They are bit-level operations performed on ordinary String values
They can only store 64 bits
They automatically compress sparse data

questions.explanation: Bitmap commands (SETBIT, GETBIT, BITCOUNT, BITOP) treat a String as an array of bits — there is no separate 'bitmap' type.

questions.prompt: What does a HyperLogLog give you?

options.text: An exact count and the ability to list all members
An approximate count of distinct elements using fixed, tiny memory
A sorted list of the most frequent elements
A way to store and retrieve large blobs

questions.explanation: A HyperLogLog estimates cardinality (distinct count) in a fixed ~12 KB with about 0.81% error; it does not store or return the individual elements.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: PFADD adds elements to a HyperLogLog; PFCOUNT returns the estimated distinct count
A HyperLogLog uses roughly the same memory whether it holds thousands or billions of elements
You can read individual elements back out of a HyperLogLog
BITOP can combine two bitmaps with AND/OR/XOR/NOT

questions.explanation: PFADD/PFCOUNT work as described, HLL memory is near-constant, and BITOP combines bitmaps. You canNOT list a HyperLogLog's members.

questions.prompt: For which task is a HyperLogLog the WRONG choice?

options.text: Reporting roughly how many unique visitors a huge site had today
Billing each customer for the exact number of distinct API callers, auditable
Estimating distinct search terms across billions of queries
Rolling daily unique estimates up into a monthly total with PFMERGE

questions.explanation: HyperLogLog is approximate (~0.81% error) and can't list members, so it's unsuitable for exact, auditable counts like billing — use a Set or a database.

questions.prompt: The command that counts the number of set (1) bits in a bitmap is ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: BITCOUNT counts the 1-bits, optionally within a byte (or BIT) range.

questions.prompt: When is a bitmap a poor fit for tracking boolean state per item?

options.text: When item IDs are dense small integers
When item IDs are large and sparse (e.g. random 64-bit numbers)
When you need to count set bits
When you want to combine two days with BITOP

questions.explanation: A bitmap's size is driven by the highest offset you set, so large, sparse IDs waste huge amounts of space. Bitmaps shine with dense integer IDs.
